title: Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar gives Google’s AI a face
content:
Google’s new Gemini 3.8 Live update lets users have conversations with the model while watching an animated AI persona respond in real time. The “Live Avatar” will lip-sync and show different facial expressions during conversations, but it’s currently only available to Gemini Enterprise customers.
Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar gives Google’s AI a face
Google’s Live Avatar can lip-sync and show different facial expressions.
As noted by Google, Live Avatar can transition between the 97 languages it supports “without degrading video fidelity or introducing visual drift.” One video shared by Google shows its Live Avatar talking in English and Japanese, with its mouth animation lining up with what it’s saying in both languages. It can also pull up information on-screen while it talks.
The launch of Live Avatar comes about a week after Google revealed its new Gemini 3.8 Live model, which the company says “processes visual inputs in near real-time.” Though Google will offer a library of preset avatars for customers to choose from, it will also allow organizations to create their own. Google says output from its Live Avatar comes with its invisible SynthID watermark alongside safeguards to “respect identity.”

report.summary: Google’s Gemini 3.8 Live adds a real-time, lip-syncing Live Avatar with facial expressions, initially for Gemini Enterprise customers, supporting 97 languages and custom avatars.
report.background: For years, voice assistants have been audio-first and chatbots text-first, but the industry is racing toward real-time multimodal AI that can see, speak, and appear on screen. Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, and Meta are all pushing low-latency voice and video interactions. Gemini 3.8 Live processes visual inputs in near real-time, and Live Avatar adds an embodied face. The enterprise-first launch reflects monetization opportunities in customer service, training, sales, and virtual agents, where brands want consistent multilingual personas. Avatars must lip-sync accurately across languages, avoid uncanny visual drift, and include identity safeguards. Google’s use of SynthID watermarking also responds to deepfake and synthetic-media concerns. The move follows avatar startups like HeyGen, Synthesia, and D-ID, but integrates the face directly into a major foundation model.
key_points: Live Avatar is a real-time animated persona that lip-syncs and shows facial expressions during conversations with Gemini 3.8 Live. It can also pull up information on-screen while talking. The experience is designed to feel like a face-to-face interaction, not just a voice or text reply, but it is currently limited to Gemini Enterprise customers.

Google says Live Avatar supports 97 languages and can switch between them without degrading video fidelity or introducing visual drift. A demo shows English and Japanese lip-sync matching speech. This matters for global enterprises that need consistent multilingual agents for support, training, or sales across regions.

Customers will get a library of preset avatars, and organizations can create their own branded personas. Output carries Google’s invisible SynthID watermark plus safeguards intended to respect identity. These controls aim to balance personalization with misuse prevention as synthetic media becomes more realistic.

The avatar arrives about a week after Gemini 3.8 Live, which Google says processes visual inputs in near real-time. Together they push Gemini from a multimodal chat model toward an embodied assistant that can see, speak, and appear on screen, though API access and pricing remain unclear.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Live Avatar signals a shift from text and voice assistants to embodied digital humans, raising the bar for real-time multimodal latency, multilingual lip-sync, and safety. Developers may need to build avatar orchestration, streaming video, identity consent, and watermark verification into enterprise apps. Regular users can expect more human-like support agents and virtual presenters, but also more convincing deepfakes and emotional manipulation risks. The enterprise-only launch means consumers won’t see it immediately, yet it pressures rivals like OpenAI, Microsoft, and avatar startups to combine foundation models with real-time rendering. If Google opens it to developers, it could become a platform for customer service, training, accessibility, and branded assistants.
report.tools: To follow this space, watch Google’s Gemini API, Vertex AI, and SynthID documentation. Open-source alternatives for real-time avatars include LivePortrait, MuseTalk, Wav2Lip, and SadTalker for lip-sync; NVIDIA Audio2Face and Unreal MetaHuman for expressive 3D characters. Commercial comparators are HeyGen, Synthesia, and D-ID. Developers can prototype with WebRTC, Whisper, and streaming TTS, then add watermarking and consent checks before deploying enterprise-facing avatars.
